bib.title: Tree-Based Methods (Chapter 8, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python)

question: How do decision trees, and ensembles of them (bagging, random forests, boosting, BART), work for regression and classification, and when do they help?

limits: Authors concede single trees are not competitive in accuracy and are non-robust; ensembles trade interpretability for accuracy.
Lab results are single random splits; authors note results change with seeds (cross-validation has variance), and boosting/RF/BART differences on gene data are within SE ~0.02.
Boosting for classification is omitted ('details are omitted'); BART shown for regression only; Bayesian derivation out of scope.
sklearn trees treat one-hot levels as separate variables, not native categorical splits.
Lab text says GBR learning_rate default is 0.001; stated in the book, not verified (sklearn's default is commonly 0.1).
practices: Grow a large tree then prune by cost-complexity, choosing alpha by K-fold CV (Algorithm 8.1, p.337).
Use Gini or entropy for growing classification trees; use classification error for pruning when accuracy is the goal (p.339).
Choose B for bagging/RF large enough that error settles; it does not overfit (p.344-345).
Use OOB error as a free test-error estimate for bagged models; with large B it is virtually LOOCV (p.345).
Use m ~ sqrt(p) for classification forests, small m when many correlated predictors (p.346-347).
Boosting: choose B by CV, lambda 0.01 or 0.001, small d (d=1 gives additive model) (p.349).
BART: K=200, B=1000, L=100 gives good out-of-box performance (p.353).
Compare trees vs linear models by CV/validation error; linear wins if truth is linear (p.341).

terms.definition: Rather than considering every possible subtree, we consider a sequence of trees indexed by a nonnegative tuning parameter alpha (minimise RSS + alpha|T|)
G = sum_k p_mk(1-p_mk), a measure of total variance across the K classes; a measure of node purity
The remaining one-third of the observations not used to fit a given bagged tree
Bagged trees where each split considers a random sample of m of the p predictors; m=p is bagging
d, number of splits per boosted tree; d splits involve at most d variables
Earlier BART iterations discarded because they tend not to give good results
